_comment: What grows in the Meadows playground, and where. ALL of it is TUNABLE. The expected feedback is 'too sparse', 'too busy', 'the trees are on the cliffs' — every one of those has to be answerable here rather than in a scene.
_comment_authored: M7 authored the actual geography and this file now reflects it. Placement here comes in FOUR kinds, and which kind a thing is is the whole of GAME_DESIGN.md §7's split between authored macro geography and procedural dressing. A `clumps`/`strays` layer is a density: how much of this, and where is it allowed. A `clump_at` layer is a density inside AUTHORED PLACES: the oak grove is at those coordinates because the road goes through it. A `route_from` layer follows a named polyline in trails.json. A `sites` layer expands buildings from data/config/settlement.json. Only the first kind is free to move when the seed changes.
_comment_clumping: Every layer clusters. Evenly-spread props at uniform scale are the readable signature of generator output — the visual rubric names it — so each layer places clumps and scatters within them, leaving clearings between. `strays` fills the gaps so the clumps do not read as islands.
_comment_pack: Quaternius Stylized Nature MegaKit (CC0), replacing Kenney's Nature Kit. The blind critic's verdict on the Kenney set was that every tree was the same tree — 'one straight tapered trunk, one 6-8 face canopy, two greens, varied only by uniform scale' — and that the far tree line read as 'a row of identical cards at near-uniform spacing along a contour: a fence of icons'. It measured mid-distance trees at 1.00:1 luminance contrast against the ground behind them, meaning invisible. This pack ships four genuinely different tree species with real bark and leaf TEXTURES and normal maps, which is what that complaint was actually about.
_comment_scale: These models are authored in METRES, unlike Kenney's which were about one unit tall and needed a 3.4x per-layer correction. So `base_scale` is near 1.0 here and mostly trims rather than multiplies. Measured with tools/measure_models.gd rather than guessed — guessing produced a meadow of knee-high trees once already.

trees._comment: The common broadleaf, 7-9m. The everyday tree of the meadow, in copses.
trees._comment_clumping: Copses, placed by rule but kept OFF the authored places: the oak grove is its own layer and the settlement stands in cleared ground. Twelve dense copses with real gaps between them reads as somebody deciding where a wood goes; twenty-six evenly spread reads as a distribution.
trees._comment_slope: Trees stop well before the rocky rises. A tree growing out of a cliff face is the cheapest way to destroy the sense that a place was authored.
trees._comment_scale: Native height is 7.0-9.4m, so this renders 5.3-13.7m. Raised from 0.55-1.35 (3.9-12.7m): the blind critic measured the tallest tree in the build at 9.8m against a key art board that wants 15-25m, and a meadow whose biggest tree is five times the player is a meadow with no vertical event in it. The common tree is the everyday one and stays under the grove oaks; the grove is where the 15-25m band is actually met.
trees._comment_clear: The spawn pad stays clear. The player's first sight of the game should not be the inside of a tree.
trees._comment_authored: Four of the fifteen copses are STATED, and they ring the oak grove. The grove's twisted oaks carry the pack's crimson autumn leaf and six stands of them alone read as one solid red mass rather than as a wood; green common trees mixed through and around them turn it into a wood with a red heart. The other eleven copses are wherever the seed puts them, which is what a copse is.
trees._comment_strays: Raised from 26. The mid-distance — roughly 80m to 250m out — was the flattest part of every frame: an unbroken pale green sheet with the authored places sitting on it and nothing between them. Strays are what fill that, because a clump reads as one object at that range and a scatter reads as a landscape.
trees._comment_variation: Height, lean and spacing all vary now, and the first two are new. The critic's charge was that the ridge trees are 'at uniform height, lean, canopy size and spacing' — a 0.75-1.45 uniform draw sounds varied and is not, because a uniform sample piles up in the middle and the eye reads the mode. `size_bias` 1.7 squares the draw toward the small end, so most trees are modest and a few are giants, which is the size distribution a real wood has. `lean_deg` tilts each trunk up to 8 degrees off plumb about its own axis.

grove._comment: THE OAK GROVE. §25 lists oak woodland patches as one of the five things the Meadows is; the milestone asks for a grove, singular, and a grove is a PLACE rather than a density. So these six stands have stated centres, the road runs through the middle of them, and they are still in the same field when the seed changes. Ancient twisted oaks, 15-19m native and far broader than anything else in the world — at twice the height of a common tree and three times the canopy, a stand of them reads from across the meadow, which is the entire job of a landmark tree.
grove._comment_count: Deliberately few. A 10,000-triangle tree is thirty times a Kenney one, and these are the biggest thing in the world — a stand of six is a landmark, forty is a forest nobody can walk through.
grove._comment_retexture: The pack's `Leaves_TwistedTree_C` is a crimson autumn leaf shared by the twisted oaks and the common bushes. Both layers now point at the green leaf and tint from there.
grove._comment_colour:
NO LONGER CRIMSON, and this reverses a call recorded here in M7.

The pack ships `Leaves_TwistedTree_C` as a saturated autumn crimson and the grove was left carrying it because the owner liked the red trees and because it was the one second hue family in the meadow. MA-05 measured what it actually costs: it is the loudest colour event in the world and it marks nothing — not a landmark, not a resource, not a boundary — 'it is where a scatter rule changed'. And the key art's palette strip has one dark oxblood and no saturated crimson at all.

The harder constraint is `data/config/palette.json`: `tether_oxblood` is RESERVED — it appears only on Team Tether banners, equipment and uniforms, never on friendly or neutral elements, because a reserved colour is what lets a player read threat at distance without a marker. A hundred deep-red trees in the meadow is that channel spent on scenery.

So the leaves take the pack's GREEN leaf texture (the same swap the bushes already use, for the same reason: no multiply turns red green) and then a warm amber modulate over it. The result is a golden-olive turning oak — the autumn READ the owner wanted, at the key art's `flower_gold`/`grass_olive` end of the palette instead of at Team Tether's.
grove._comment_where: Sited astride the trail's western half, between the pond and the spawn, so the player walks THROUGH the grove on the way to the water. It is also dead centre of the survey's `03` viewpoint, which is the frame the critic said had nothing in it to walk toward.
grove._comment_scale: 15.7-19.0m native, rendering 11.3-21.8m. It was base_scale 0.85 at 0.55-1.00, which is 7.3-16m — and the critic's measurement of the tallest tree in the build at 9.8m against the board's 15-25m was taken with that in force. These are the trees that meet the band.

deadfall._comment: Dead trees and mushrooms. The dead trees are 9-13m bare silhouettes and do a job no living tree can: they break a green tree line with a grey vertical, which is most of what stops a treeline reading as a hedge.

bushes._comment: The middle layer. Without something between grass height and tree height the ground reads as a lawn with poles on it. Ferns and broad plants included, because undergrowth banked at the base of a tree is what makes a copse read as a wood rather than as trees standing on a lawn.
bushes._comment_retexture: Bush_Common and Bush_Common_Flowers use the material `Leaves_TwistedTree`, whose texture the pack ships CRIMSON — it is the autumn variant of the twisted oak. Unswapped, every bush in the meadow came out blood red, and no colour multiply turns red into green. This points them at the pack's own green leaf instead.
bushes._comment_shared_models: The retint and retexture are the UNION used by every layer that shares a model with another: grass, bushes, both tree skirts and the grove understory all carry exactly these two keys. Batches are grouped by MESH, so a model used by two layers can only carry one material — vegetation.gd warns when two layers ask for different things, and it was firing four times a build on models whose layers disagreed only by omission. Keying on the MATERIAL name means one shared dictionary serves all of them: `Grass` only exists on the tufts, `Leaves_TwistedTree` only on the bushes.

grass._comment: Tufts, not a ground texture. These are what make the terrain read as a meadow rather than as a painted surface, and they are the layer whose density most separates these frames from the reference — Palworld's meadows measure 3-9% featureless ground against this build's 56-66%.
grass._comment_scale: The source tufts are 1.3-1.9m, which is head-high grass. Trimmed to roughly knee height, with a 2.5x spread.
grass._comment_shadow: No shadow. Thousands of tufts each casting one overlap into a black carpet on terrain that does receive — measured at luminance 0.068 in the near field against 0.27-0.60 across the references. A blade's shadow is not information at this scale.
grass._comment_clearings: Walked straight through, so it cannot hide a creature or block a camera — the arena clearings do not apply. Stripping it left the spawn as forty metres of bare ground in the foreground of every survey frame.
grass._comment_density:
THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE NUMBER IN THIS FILE, per MA-05: 'the frame is empty where the references are full, and the emptiness is the ground plane — most of the picture.' The bottom half of `01-spawn-outward` held about three dozen flower sprites across 800x450 and nothing else, and the ground half measured a value standard deviation of 0.09-0.11 against roughly 0.20 across the five Palworld references.

MOSTLY STRAYS, and that is a correction of a first attempt that went the other way. Every other layer in this file clusters, because evenly-spread props at uniform scale are the signature of generator output — but that argument is about OBJECTS. Grass is not an object, it is the surface, and a real meadow has grass everywhere with denser and thinner patches through it. Putting 85% of the tufts into 520 tight clumps produced exactly the failure you would expect: dense islands, and a spawn camera standing between two of them looking at bare ground. So the clumps are now the VARIATION on top of a base coverage that exists everywhere.

The tufts are also bigger — 0.33-0.72m rendered against the old 0.13-0.31m. Meadow grass is 0.2-0.5m against a 1.80m trainer and the taller model reaches 0.72m, so this is still grass rather than wheat; the old size was ankle fuzz that could not read at any distance.

WHAT THIS STILL IS NOT is Palworld's coverage, and the arithmetic says why. Reference density is roughly a tuft per square metre; over a 512m playground that is 260,000 instances, and these models are 155-326 triangles each because they are modelled tufts rather than the two-triangle cards an engine-side grass system uses. Sixty thousand is what fits. Closing the rest of that gap is a different technique — Terrain3DInstancer's per-region streaming, or camera-relative placement — not a bigger number here.
grass._comment_base_scale: Corrects the PACK's authoring scale, and was left at 1.0 while it should never have been. Round 4 measured grass tufts at 1.9m and a wildflower at 2.1m against the 1.80m trainer — head height on the player. Confirmed from the source models: Grass_Common_Tall is 1.87m native, Flower_4_Group is 2.49m, and the layer scales were multiplying those by 0.26-0.78 rather than correcting them. The critic's reading of the damage is the reason this is the first fix and not a small one: it 'makes the world read as a miniature diorama, makes the trainer read as a doll, and lets very few instances cover the ground — which is part of why the density looks thin.' Meadow grass is 0.2-0.5m.
grass._comment_offtrail: The trail is the one place nothing grows. A line of stones with meadow closing over it from both sides is a decorative border, not a path — what reads as trodden ground is the ABSENCE of grass on it, and the bake paints the same strip brown underneath.
grass._comment_density_round2: Raised with the ground fix. The previous numbers were tuned against a meadow whose flat ground was rendering the ROCK texture, and 'the grass looks thin' was competing with 'the ground looks like cracked stone'. With real grass under it the near field reads as a mown lawn at that density. 150 clumps of 90 plus 3200 strays is 16,700 tufts, and the scale is up from 0.16-0.47m to 0.20-0.58m — still meadow grass against a 1.8m trainer, which is the measurement round 4 was actually about.
grass._comment_cost: About 30,000 tufts against the previous 16,700, at 155-326 triangles each. That is affordable ONLY because vegetation.gd now splits each model into 64m spatial cells, so the frustum discards most of it — before that change every tuft in the world was drawn from every camera. On the Ally, pull `ground_cover_density` back rather than editing these.
grass._comment_retint: A green multiply over the pack's own grass texture. The tufts were rendering paler and yellower than the ground they stand on, which makes them read as separate objects scattered on a lawn rather than as the lawn. Darker also buys the thing MA-05 actually measured: value variation. Ground-half standard deviation was 0.09-0.11 against roughly 0.20 across the references, and geometry that is the same value as the ground it covers contributes nothing to it.
grass._comment_shared_models: The retint and retexture are the UNION used by every layer that shares a model with another: grass, bushes, both tree skirts and the grove understory all carry exactly these two keys. Batches are grouped by MESH, so a model used by two layers can only carry one material — vegetation.gd warns when two layers ask for different things, and it was firing four times a build on models whose layers disagreed only by omission. Keying on the MATERIAL name means one shared dictionary serves all of them: `Grass` only exists on the tufts, `Leaves_TwistedTree` only on the bushes.

drygrass._comment: The wispy tufts, warmer and looser, in their own patches. Two grass textures where there was one. The critic counted 2 hue families against the key art board's 6 and said the board's golds appear nowhere below the horizon; this and the flowers are where the warm end comes from.
drygrass._comment_retint: A warm straw modulate over the grass texture. Multiplies, so it stays light. Pulled back from #e8d89a, which came out as bright yellow spikes against the new green ground rather than as dry grass.
drygrass._comment_base_scale: Same correction as `grass`; Grass_Wispy_Tall is 1.67m native.

flowers._comment: Colour accents, clustered hard. Wildflowers grow in patches; spread evenly they read as confetti. Clover is in here because a flower patch with nothing between the blooms reads as pins in a board.
flowers._comment_density: The critic measured saturated non-green pixels below the horizon at 0.000%-0.035% of frame against a design brief that says 'wildflower meadows', and found ZERO in one frame out of 921,600 pixels. A colour accent nobody can see is not an accent.
flowers._comment_base_scale: Same correction. Flower_4_Group is 2.49m native — taller than the player before this.
flowers._comment_upright: The clovers are gone from this layer. MA-05: 'Flower billboards lie flat, reading as smears on the ground rather than upright plants.' `Clover_1`/`Clover_2` are ground-hugging leaf mats and at this layer's scale they are exactly that smear — a flower layer should be things standing up. They stay in the tree skirts, where a leaf mat at the foot of a trunk is the right object.

rocks._comment: Rocks go where trees will not: they are the layer that makes the steep ground read as stone rather than as grass at an angle. The critic found the previous rocks read as 'dollops of moss' because their lit top face was the same hue as grass — these carry a real rock texture instead of a tinted flat colour.
rocks._comment_slope: The only layer with a MINIMUM slope as well as a maximum, so boulders gather on the shoulders and rises where they belong instead of sitting on flat grass like dropped props.
rocks._comment_outcrops: CLUSTERED INTO OUTCROPS. MA-05 counted '~25 near-identical grey rocks at near-identical scale, evenly distributed across the slope like sprinkles, including several on the steepest face where nothing would rest'. Both halves of that are fixed here: far fewer, far tighter clumps with almost no strays, so a boulder belongs to a group; and a 0.3-2.6 scale range biased small, so a group has one big stone and a scatter of small ones instead of twenty-five of the same rock. The maximum slope comes down as well — nothing rests on a 44-degree face, and `bluff_scree` is the layer that is allowed to be steep because scree genuinely is.

path_stones._comment: Flat rock plates laid along an AUTHORED LINE. Was a scatter, with a comment admitting 'not a path yet' — and a density can never become one: every other layer answers 'how much of this and where is it allowed', where a path answers 'from here, to there, past that'.
path_stones._comment_why: The critic measured one frame at 0.7% desaturated pixels against 18-30% across the Palworld references — 'no stone, no wood, no built thing, no path anywhere in that frame' — and its third-ranked gap was that the eye is given nothing to do. A path is the standard answer to the second half of that: it says where to enter a landscape and where you are being led.
path_stones._comment_route: World coordinates now live in data/config/trails.json and NOT here, because three systems need this polyline and they have to agree to the metre: the terrain bake paints the worn track into the ground colour along it, this lays the stones on it, and every ground-cover layer refuses to grow within `off_trail` of it. Three copies is three polylines the moment anybody moves one. Catmull-Rom through the waypoints, so it bends rather than turning corners, and every stone takes its height from the field so it drapes over the ground instead of cutting through it.
path_stones._comment_random: What is random is only the scatter ACROSS the line — how far each stone strays from the centre, its yaw and its size — so the result reads as trodden rather than as tiling.
path_stones._comment_clear: Small rather than zero. The road passes the spawn at about seven metres and the player's first step should be onto it — arriving somewhere rather than being dropped in a field. Zero would fail test_every_layer_keeps_the_spawn_clear_at_all, and that test is right even here: it leaves the few metres the player is actually standing on unpaved, which no road should be paving anyway.
path_stones._comment_slope: Raised from 26. The last stretch of the road climbs out of the settlement toward the stronghold bluff and genuinely crosses ground at 29 degrees; at 26 the stones simply stopped being drawn there, which reads as a path that evaporates rather than as a path that climbs. The bake names every waypoint the stones would refuse, which is how this was found.
path_stones._comment_stones_round2: Smaller, closer to the centreline, denser along it, and knocked off white. The first render had them at 0.6-1.4 scale wandering 1.5m either side of the line at one per step: they came out as bright white clumps with two-metre gaps, which reads as scattered marshmallows rather than as a laid path. The pack's `PathRocks` material is a very light stone and it was the brightest thing in the frame; the retint takes it to a warm grey that belongs next to a dirt track.

tree_skirt._comment: Undergrowth banked around the base of every common tree. NOT a scatter: this layer reads the placements of the layer it names and rings each one, so every trunk gets growth rather than some trunks getting lucky.
tree_skirt._comment_why: The critic's artefact list, four frames running: trunks 'meet the ground with a straight cut, no root flare, no AO, no tuft'. A tree model ends at a flat disc where the trunk was cut off, and a scatter that places ferns independently of trees only ever puts one near a trunk by accident. Nothing here changes the trees; it hides the join, which is the entire job.
tree_skirt._comment_scale: Small and low. This is ROOT FLARE, not a second bush layer — anything you notice as a plant in its own right has grown too big and reads as clutter around the trunk rather than as part of it.
tree_skirt._comment_ring: An ANNULUS, not a disc. `skirt_inner` keeps tufts off the trunk itself, where the trunk would swallow them and they would cost a draw call for nothing. Both radii are multiplied by the host tree's own scale, so a big tree gets a wide skirt.
tree_skirt._comment_clear: Inherited from the host layer, minus this skirt's widest ring. A skirt cannot reach the spawn pad unless its host tree does, so this is implied rather than independent — but 'implied' is exactly what test_every_layer_keeps_the_spawn_clear_at_all refuses to accept, and it is right to. An invariant that holds because of a relationship between two config blocks is one config edit away from not holding.
tree_skirt._comment_base_scale: Same pack, same correction — the skirt models are the oversized grass and clover.
tree_skirt._comment_shared_models: The retint and retexture are the UNION used by every layer that shares a model with another: grass, bushes, both tree skirts and the grove understory all carry exactly these two keys. Batches are grouped by MESH, so a model used by two layers can only carry one material — vegetation.gd warns when two layers ask for different things, and it was firing four times a build on models whose layers disagreed only by omission. Keying on the MATERIAL name means one shared dictionary serves all of them: `Grass` only exists on the tufts, `Leaves_TwistedTree` only on the bushes.
tree_skirt._comment_no_mushroom: Mushroom_Common was dropped from the skirts because it is also in `deadfall`, which carries no retint, and a model in two layers can only carry one material — the build warned about it every time. A mushroom at a trunk base is a nice detail and not worth a standing warning; `deadfall` still places them across the meadow.

grove_skirt._comment: The same root flare for the grove oaks, which need it most: they are the widest trunks in the world, so their straight cut into the ground is the most visible one.
grove_skirt._comment_clear: Inherited from the host layer, minus this skirt's widest ring. A skirt cannot reach the spawn pad unless its host tree does, so this is implied rather than independent — but 'implied' is exactly what test_every_layer_keeps_the_spawn_clear_at_all refuses to accept, and it is right to. An invariant that holds because of a relationship between two config blocks is one config edit away from not holding.
grove_skirt._comment_base_scale: Same correction, a little larger because a grove oak's flare should out-scale a common tree's.
grove_skirt._comment_shared_models: The retint and retexture are the UNION used by every layer that shares a model with another: grass, bushes, both tree skirts and the grove understory all carry exactly these two keys. Batches are grouped by MESH, so a model used by two layers can only carry one material — vegetation.gd warns when two layers ask for different things, and it was firing four times a build on models whose layers disagreed only by omission. Keying on the MATERIAL name means one shared dictionary serves all of them: `Grass` only exists on the tufts, `Leaves_TwistedTree` only on the bushes.
grove_skirt._comment_no_mushroom: Mushroom_Common was dropped from the skirts because it is also in `deadfall`, which carries no retint, and a model in two layers can only carry one material — the build warned about it every time. A mushroom at a trunk base is a nice detail and not worth a standing warning; `deadfall` still places them across the meadow.

grove_under._comment: THE GROVE'S UNDERSTORY. MA-05: 'The grove has no understory, no shadow pooling, and bright unshaded grass visible straight through it — a grove is a place; this is a tree density value.' Six stands of oaks standing on the same lawn as the open meadow is a tree count, not a wood. This is the tier between the grass and the canopy: shrubs and broad ferns banked under the oaks, dense enough that the ground under the grove is a different surface from the ground outside it. Sited on the grove's own authored centres, so it moves with the grove and not with the seed.
grove_under._comment_retexture: Same crimson leaf material as the bushes and for the same reason: unswapped, every shrub in the grove comes out blood red.
grove_under._comment_shared_models: The retint and retexture are the UNION used by every layer that shares a model with another: grass, bushes, both tree skirts and the grove understory all carry exactly these two keys. Batches are grouped by MESH, so a model used by two layers can only carry one material — vegetation.gd warns when two layers ask for different things, and it was firing four times a build on models whose layers disagreed only by omission. Keying on the MATERIAL name means one shared dictionary serves all of them: `Grass` only exists on the tufts, `Leaves_TwistedTree` only on the bushes.

grove_timber._comment: FALLEN TIMBER, on the grove floor. The same dead trunks the `deadfall` layer stands upright, laid over at 68-104 degrees by `lean_min_deg`. A wood with nothing on its floor reads as trees planted on a lawn; a log is the cheapest object that says this ground has been here a long time. Also the only horizontal mass anywhere in the near field, which is half of why the ground half of every frame measured flat.

outcrop._comment: THE ROCK OUTCROP. A tor at (-138,-46) with a boulder field on and around it. The terrain supplies the landform — a short steep-toed rise, sharpness 2.8 — and this supplies the stone that makes it read as geology rather than as a green pimple. Sited on the sightline of the survey's `04` camera, which is the frame that had nothing in it.
outcrop._comment_scale: Big. Rock_Medium is 3.0-3.5m native and these render 3.6-9.6m, which is house-sized — an outcrop made of knee-high pebbles is a gravel patch. They are the only rocks in the world at this scale and that is what makes the place identifiable from a distance.

bluff_scree._comment: Scree on the stronghold bluff's flanks. Killing the rock texture out of the auto shader (see terrain_playground.json) fixed the black veins across the whole meadow and cost the one place that genuinely wanted stone: the bluff came out a smooth tan dome, which reads as a bald hill rather than as a crag. Boulders put the stone back where it belongs — as geometry standing on the slope rather than as a texture smeared across every lawn in the world.
bluff_scree._comment_slope: The only layer allowed above 44 degrees. `min_slope_deg` keeps it OFF the summit, which is the ruin's ground, and off the meadow at the foot.

buildings._comment: THE AUTHORED ARCHITECTURE. Layouts live in data/config/settlement.json as grid coordinates and piece ids from the player's own build catalogue; this layer only says which sites are in the world and how they are rendered and collided. See scatter_rules.buildings_for().
buildings._comment_models: Every model any site can use has to be listed here, for two reasons that are both load-bearing: `vegetation.gd` recovers a prop's LAYER by looking its model up in these lists, which is how a wall gets box collision instead of a tree's cylinder; and test_every_model_named_in_the_config_exists reads exactly this list. The boulders the stronghold uses as standing stones are deliberately NOT here — they resolve to the `rocks` layer, which is the correct treatment for a rock.
buildings._comment_collision: Real box colliders, taken from the catalogue's own measured `collider_centre`/`collider_extents`, rotated with the piece. A cylinder is right for a tree trunk and wrong for a 2m wall — walk into a cottage with cylinder collision and you slide around the outside of an invisible barrel.

world_edge_fence._comment: THE VISIBLE EDGE OF THE PLAYABLE WORLD. The baked terrain ends at ±256m (terrain_playground.json `world_size`) and beyond it there is no heightfield and no collision — a player who sprints past the rim simply falls out of the world, which the owner did. The honest fix has two halves: player_controller.gd pushes back softly inside the rim, and this layer is the half you can SEE — a kit fence ring at ±250m, six metres inside the edge, so the boundary is a thing somebody built rather than an invisible force. The same `route` mechanism as path_stones, with `route_align` so each panel takes the line's heading instead of a random yaw — a fence with random yaw is scattered planks.
world_edge_fence._comment_reachable: The whole ring is reachable ground: sampled every 2m around the ±250m square with playground_heightfield, the worst slope on it is 23 degrees against the character's 45-degree limit, so there is no stretch a player cannot walk to and the fence runs the full perimeter. `max_slope_deg` 30 stands guard anyway — if a future terrain retune steepens a stretch past what a fence can stand on, panels drop out there rather than hanging in the air, and the push-back still covers the gap.
world_edge_fence._comment_cost: THE PROP-COUNT COST, stated: four 500m sides at one 2.02m panel per step is ~980 panels. They share one mesh with the settlement's fences, so vegetation.gd batches them into ONE model group, chunked into 64m cells (~35 populated cells on the ring) — a handful of draw calls, almost all frustum-culled from anywhere inside the meadow. Collision is ~980 static box shapes in one body, which the physics server holds without complaint next to the settlement's own hundreds.
world_edge_fence._comment_not_a_wall: The panel is 0.81m tall and a 1.35m jump clears it. Deliberate: the fence is the SIGN, the push-back in player_controller is the boundary. A fence tall enough to be the boundary itself would be a wall around the world, which is the exact reading grandpa's paddock comment warns against — this one gets to exist because the world genuinely does end here.
world_edge_fence._comment_shared_model: Prop_WoodenFence_Single is also in the `buildings` layer's model list, DELIBERATELY, and rendering/collision settings for the shared batch come from `buildings` (vegetation.gd's `_layer_for` takes the first layer naming a model): piece-measured box collision, shadows on. This block only decides WHERE the ring's panels stand. No retint and no retexture here, matching `buildings`, so the shared-model warning stays quiet.

_comment_retint: Global material remap, applied to every layer unless a layer overrides it. The pack's bark textures are a pale salmon and read as pink trunks in every frame (D18's open item 4); `albedo_color` multiplies, so a warm grey pulls them to brown without touching the texture's own grain. Leaves and rock pass through unmapped.
_comment_collision: Layers marked `collides` get real static collision. Two reasons, and the second is the urgent one: a tree you can walk through reads as a hologram, and — because the camera's SpringArm3D only stops at things with collision — a bush with none lets the camera end up INSIDE it. Two survey frames came back showing nothing but green because the camera was inside a bush during a fight. Grass and flowers must never collide; you walk through those.
_comment_clearings: Open ground kept clear of every layer that can BLOCK. These match the wild pal spawn points in scripts/combat/encounter_director.gd, because a fight starts where a creature is standing and the arena is 11m across: without this, the trees are inside the arena and stand between the camera and the fight. The radius is arena radius plus margin.

_comment_density_dial: GROUND COVER DENSITY — the ROG Ally dial, and the only tunable in this file that is about the machine rather than about the meadow. Layers marked `density_scaled` multiply their `per_clump` and `strays` by it. 1.0 is the desktop look measured against the Palworld references; 0.5 halves the tuft count for the handheld and changes nothing else about the world's composition, because the CLUMP COUNT is untouched — the patches stay where they are and get thinner, rather than the meadow losing patches. TUNABLE.
_comment_batch_cell: Metres per spatial batching cell in vegetation.gd. A MultiMesh has one bounding box, so a single 30,000-instance grass batch is drawn in full from every camera in the world — which is the ceiling that kept the ground empty. Cutting each model into cells gives the frustum something to throw away, at the cost of one draw call per populated cell. Bigger = fewer draw calls and worse culling. TUNABLE.
